name: Vabelon: Lightweight Multilingual, Hreflang Tags & Language Switcher
author: Renzo Johnson

sections.description:
Run a bilingual or multilingual WordPress site with translations you write yourself. Vabelon gives each language its own addresses, adds hreflang tags and prints a language switcher. Your translations are ordinary pages and posts, so they stay in your database and keep working with your theme and editor.

Vabelon is a small multilanguage plugin. It has no automatic translation, no AI, no account and no external service. It adds one settings screen and one box in the editor.

What you get

  • Languages you define. Add each language under Settings > Vabelon with its address prefix, WordPress locale, hreflang code and name. Pick one as the default.
  • One page per language. Give a page or post a language in the editor, then link it to its translation. Each translation is a normal post you write and publish.
  • Language addresses. Translations live under their prefix, such as /es/sobre-nosotros. The default language keeps your current addresses.
  • A translated front page. Link a translation to your static front page and it answers at the language home, such as /es.
  • Hreflang tags. Every page with a published translation lists its alternates in the page head, with x-default pointing at the default language.
  • The right page language. WordPress runs in the language of the address, so the lang attribute and your theme’s own strings follow the visitor’s language.
  • A language switcher. Place [vabelon_switcher] wherever shortcodes work. It links each page to its translation and marks the current language.

Built to stay out of your way

  • Your content stays yours. Translations are regular posts and pages. Remove Vabelon and every page is still there.
  • Existing content keeps working. Content with no language is shown as the default language, so you can translate one page at a time.
  • Nothing leaves your site. Vabelon makes no outside requests and stores no visitor data.
  • Style the switcher your way. The switcher prints clean list markup with BEM classes and no styles of its own.
  • Developer friendly. Add your own post types with the vabelon_post_types filter.

See the features or read the documentation.
sections.installation:
1. In WordPress, go to Plugins > Add New and search for “Vabelon”.
  2. Click Install Now, then Activate.
  3. Open Settings > Vabelon, add your languages and choose the default.
  4. Edit a page, pick its language in the Vabelon box and save.
  5. Write the translation as a new page, then link the two by entering the translation’s ID in the Vabelon box.
  6. Add [vabelon_switcher] to your header, a widget or a page.

For a ZIP installation, go to Plugins > Add New > Upload Plugin, select your Vabelon ZIP, install it and activate it.

Vabelon requires WordPress 6.2 or later and PHP 7.4 or later. Follow the install and activate guide for each step with examples.
sections.faq:
Does Vabelon translate my content automatically?

No. You write each translation, or paste one you had translated. Vabelon organizes the languages, addresses, hreflang tags and switcher around the pages you publish.

How do I make my WordPress site bilingual?

Add two languages under Settings > Vabelon, give each page its language, and link every page to its translation. See add your languages and link translations.

What do the addresses of translated pages look like?

Each language except the default has a prefix. A Spanish page lives at an address such as /es/contacto, and the Spanish home is /es. Read more about language addresses.

Does Vabelon add hreflang tags?

Yes. A page with at least one published translation lists every language version and an x-default entry. Pages without a translation print no hreflang tags. See hreflang and page language.

How do I add the language switcher?

Use the [vabelon_switcher] shortcode in a page, a widget or your theme. The language switcher guide shows the markup, and hooks and CSS classes lists the classes to style.

Can I translate my front page?

Yes, when your site uses a static front page. Link a translation to it and that translation becomes the home of its language. See translated front page.

What happens to the pages I already have?

Nothing changes. Pages without a language are treated as the default language and keep their addresses. See existing content.

Does it work with custom post types?

Posts and pages are supported out of the box. Add other post types with the vabelon_post_types filter, described in hooks and CSS classes.

What happens when I remove Vabelon?

Deleting the plugin removes its settings and language labels. Your pages and posts, including every translation, stay in WordPress. See removing Vabelon.

Where do I get help, ask a question or request a feature?

Start with the documentation and the frequently asked questions. For support, visit vabelon.com/support. For questions and feature requests, contact us.
